Evaluating a multilevel latent profile model with the latents R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/evaluation.Rmd
evaluation.Rmd

A fitted mixture model is evaluated on four questions: whether the estimation found a stable solution, how clearly observations and groups are classified, whether the indicators are independent within profiles as the model assumes, and whether a different number of profiles or group classes fits better. These questions follow current guidance for latent profile analysis (Spurk et al., 2020; Scrucca et al., 2024), and they matter because the profiles of a person-centred model are interpreted as substantive subgroups (Saqr et al., 2024). This guide shows the functions that answer each of them for a two-level model.

Data

course_engagement has one row per course enrolment: 1,422 enrolments from 106 students. student identifies the group, and five activity measures (browse, lectures, forum_read, forum_post, attendance) are the indicators, each standardized within course.

library(latents)

The model to evaluate

multilpa() fits the model, with vars for the indicators, id for the group, n_profiles for the number of profiles, n_group_classes for the number of group classes, n_starts for the number of random EM starts, and seed for reproducible starts. The model evaluated first uses the default diagonal covariance structure.

fit <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                         "attendance"),
                id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                n_starts = 3, seed = 1)

Estimation

get_results() with "model" reports the convergence of the fit. converged reports convergence of the best start, boundary whether a variance reached its lower bound, and n_best_replicated how many starts reached the best log likelihood. A variance at its lower bound in a profile of about one observation is a degenerate solution; fitting with boundary = "exclude" keeps the best start without one. A profile with fewer effective members than its own means and variances raises a latents_thin_profiles warning: its variances are poorly determined, so inspect its covariance diagnostics before interpreting it.

get_results(fit, "model")
#>   n_observations n_informative n_groups n_profiles n_group_classes centering scaling
#> 1           1422          1422      106          2               2      none    none
#>   covariance_structure n_parameters n_parameters_with_measurement log_likelihood   aic bic_groups
#> 1                  VVI           23                            23          -8440 16926      16987
#>   bic_individual converged iterations boundary small_classes best_start n_best_replicated weights
#> 1          17047      TRUE          9    FALSE         FALSE          1                 3    <NA>

get_results() with "starts" reports every start.

get_results(fit, "starts")
#>   start log_likelihood converged iterations error boundary
#> 1     1          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE
#> 2     2          -8440      TRUE         12  <NA>    FALSE
#> 3     3          -8440      TRUE          9  <NA>    FALSE

sensitivity() refits the model from the seeds given in seeds and reports whether they reach the same solution. optimum numbers the distinct maxima found, and agreement is the share of observations assigned as in the original fit, after matching the arbitrary profile labels.

sensitivity(fit, seeds = 1:3)
#>   seed log_likelihood converged iterations optimum best agreement
#> 1    1          -8440      TRUE          9       1 TRUE         1
#> 2    2          -8440      TRUE          9       1 TRUE         1
#> 3    3          -8440      TRUE          9       1 TRUE         1

All three starts reach the log likelihood of -8440, and all three seeds reach it with identical assignments, so the solution does not depend on the starting values.

Classification

get_results() with "entropy" reports the relative entropy (Ramaswamy et al., 1993) for observations and for groups: 1 means every case is assigned with certainty, 0 means no separation.

get_results(fit, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         2    1422       60.94            0.938
#> 2      groups         2     106        4.43            0.940

get_results() with "classification" reports the classification quality of every class. n_modal is the number of cases assigned to the class, average_posterior the mean posterior probability of those cases, and odds_correct_classification compares that certainty with the class’s size (Nagin, 2005).

get_results(fit, "classification")
#>         level class n_modal proportion_modal estimated_n estimated_proportion average_posterior
#> 1 individuals     1     836            0.588       834.1                0.587             0.985
#> 2 individuals     2     586            0.412       587.9                0.413             0.982
#> 3      groups     1      35            0.330        34.5                0.325             0.969
#> 4      groups     2      71            0.670        71.5                0.675             0.992
#>   odds_correct_classification
#> 1                        46.1
#> 2                        76.4
#> 3                        64.8
#> 4                        59.9

Relative entropy is 0.938 for the enrolments and 0.940 for the students, and the average posterior probabilities of the two profiles are 0.985 and 0.982: the classification is clear at both levels.

plot_diagnostics() draws the uncertainty: what = "entropy" the per-case uncertainty within each profile, and what = "avepp" the average posterior of each assigned class across all classes.

plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "entropy")

plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "avepp")

Local independence

The default model assumes the indicators are independent within a profile. get_results() with "residuals" tests this: residual is the correlation between two indicators that the profiles leave unexplained, and by = "overall" pools the profiles. The p-values are approximate and are adjusted for multiple testing (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

get_results(fit, "residuals", by = "overall")
#>    profile indicator_1 indicator_2     kind observed expected residual effective_n statistic df
#> 1  overall  forum_read  attendance gaussian  0.21588        0  0.21588        1422    8.2620 NA
#> 2  overall    lectures  attendance gaussian  0.19234        0  0.19234        1422    7.3369 NA

#> 7  overall      browse    lectures gaussian -0.02126        0 -0.02126        1422   -0.8009 NA
#> 8  overall  forum_read  forum_post gaussian  0.01986        0  0.01986        1422    0.7483 NA
#> 9  overall    lectures  forum_post gaussian  0.01710        0  0.01710        1422    0.6440 NA
#> 10 overall    lectures  forum_read gaussian  0.00193        0  0.00193        1422    0.0725 NA
#>     p_value p_adjusted
#> 1  1.43e-16   1.43e-15
#> 2  2.19e-13   1.09e-12
#> 3  5.78e-12   1.93e-11

#> 10 9.42e-01   9.42e-01

The four largest residuals all involve attendance (0.17 to 0.22, adjusted p-values below 0.001), so the assumption does not hold for these data; attendance is generated from the four click measures (?course_engagement). covariance_model = "full" relaxes the assumption by estimating the covariances between indicators within each profile, and get_results() with "information_criteria" compares the two models; lower values are better.

full <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                 vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                          "attendance"),
                 id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                 covariance_model = "full", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
get_results(fit, "information_criteria")
#>   log_likelihood n_parameters   aic   kic bic_groups bic_individual sabic_groups sabic_individual
#> 1          -8440           23 16926 16952      16987          17047        16914            16974
#>   caic_groups caic_individual awe_groups awe_individual icl_groups icl_individual clc_groups

#>   clc_individual
#> 1          17009
get_results(full, "information_criteria")

#> 1       16870           16981      17346          17570      17017          17128      16816
#>   clc_individual
#> 1          16816
get_results(full, "residuals", by = "overall")

The full model lowers the BIC with students as units from 16,987 to 16,827. Its residuals are zero, because it estimates every within-profile covariance; the residual check is informative only for a model that restricts them. The full model is the one to evaluate further.

Number of profiles and group classes

enumerate_classes() compares numbers of profiles and group classes, with n_profiles and n_group_classes for the counts to cross. It crosses the counts with four covariance structures, equal or varying variances with and without covariances, fits every combination, and does not choose a model.

candidates <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement,
                                vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                                         "forum_post", "attendance"),
                                id = "student", n_profiles = 2:4,
                                n_group_classes = 1:3, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
#> Warning: Profile 2: 18.6 Gaussian membership mass for 20 free means and variances. This is a
#> conservative diagnostic, not an identification test; inspect the Gaussian covariance diagnostics.

get_results() with "best" gives the candidate that minimizes each criterion. Criteria that depend on a sample size are reported with the number of groups and with the number of observations.

get_results(candidates, "best")
#>    criterion  convention             candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> profiles4_groups3_VVV          4               3   VVV 16656
#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles2_groups3_VVV          2               3   VVV 16729
#> 3        bic      groups profiles2_groups3_VVV          2               3   VVV 16801
#> 4        bic individuals profiles2_groups3_EEE          2               3   EEE 16900
#> 5      sabic      groups profiles4_groups3_VVV          4               3   VVV 16611
#> 6      sabic individuals profiles2_groups3_VVV          2               3   VVV 16775
#> 7       caic      groups profiles3_groups3_EEE          3               3   EEE 16844
#> 8       caic individuals profiles2_groups3_EEE          2               3   EEE 16930
#> 9        awe      groups profiles2_groups2_EEE          2               2   EEE 17267
#> 10       awe individuals profiles2_groups2_VVI          2               2   VVI 17412
#> 11       icl      groups profiles2_groups3_VVV          2               3   VVV 17015
#> 12       icl individuals profiles2_groups3_EEE          2               3   EEE 17122
#> 13       clc      groups profiles3_groups2_VVV          3               2   VVV 16792
#> 14       clc individuals profiles3_groups2_VVV          3               2   VVV 16792

The BIC (Schwarz, 1978) with students as units is lowest for two profiles, three group classes and the VVV structure, and most criteria select two profiles with a structure that estimates covariances. The Class enumeration article examines the choice between two and three group classes on these data.

plot_enumeration() draws one criterion across the grid, named in what; what = "all" draws every criterion.

plot_enumeration(candidates, what = "bic_groups")

get_candidate() takes one candidate out of the grid as a fitted model, given by its n_profiles, n_group_classes and model.

get_candidate(candidates, n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 3, model = "VVV")
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 2 profiles, 3 group classes
#> 1422 individuals in 106 groups; varying full residual covariance (VVV)
#> Log likelihood: -8295.382659 | AIC: 16680.765 | BIC (groups): 16800.620
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 18 | best log likelihood reached by 3 of 3 starts (3 converged)
#> Smallest standardized Gaussian eigenvalue: 0.2721 (profiles, profile_2); Gaussian mass: 589.5; weight effective n: 616.
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 58.5% (833)   profile_2 41.5% (589)
#> Group classes group_class_1 29.0% (31)   group_class_2 24.9% (26)   group_class_3 46.0% (49)
#>

#>    lectures     0.428    -0.605

#>

Parameter uncertainty

parameter_inference() returns standard errors and 95% Wald intervals; with vcov_type = "robust", the standard errors are clustered on groups. The first ten rows of each, for the full model:

Reference

The calls below list other evaluation functions and views. Each comment states what the call returns.

get_results(fit, "information_criteria", format = "long")  # one row per criterion
get_results(fit, "average_posteriors")          # mean posterior by assigned class
get_results(fit, "classification_errors")       # P(assigned class | true class)
get_results(fit, "residuals")                   # residuals within each profile
get_results(candidates, "candidates")           # the full enumeration grid
summary(candidates)                             # every grid table, truncated
bootstrap_lrt(full, get_candidate(candidates, n_profiles = 2,
                                 n_group_classes = 3, model = "VVV"),
              iter = 199, seed = 42)            # bootstrap test of one more class (slow)
enumerate_classes(course_engagement, vars = c("browse", "lectures"),
                  id = "student", n_profiles = 2:3,
                  model = c("VVI", "VVV"))      # crossing covariance models (slow)
confint(fit)                                    # confidence intervals
vcov(fit, vcov_type = "robust")                 # robust covariance matrix
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "posteriors")                  # posterior of each assigned profile
plot_profiles(fit, what = "bars")                        # profile means with 95% intervals
diagnostics(fit)                                # all classification diagnostics

Limits

  • Information criteria compare the candidates fitted, not all possible models.
  • Classification measures describe the fitted model; a misspecified model can still classify sharply.
  • Wald intervals assume a converged fit with no variance at its bound, and are conditional on the chosen numbers of profiles and classes.
  • Unmodelled dependence between indicators can make extra classes look better.
